Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Lung Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
The first question for any thoracic patient is what kind of lung cancer is this? Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the US, and most cases are found late because they cause no symptoms early on. Before anatomy, imaging, or treatment, get three things straight: the two diseases hiding under one name (NSCLC vs SCLC), what raises a person's risk, and why the biopsy result goes beyond histology. A patient's smoking history, histology, and driver mutation can completely change the treatment pathway.

Two Diseases Under One Name: NSCLC vs SCLC

Most lung cancers
Non-small cell (NSCLC)
  • Mainly adenocarcinoma and squamous cell
  • Staged with TNM
  • Early stage is curable with surgery or SBRT
  • Systemic therapy increasingly driven by driver mutations and PD-L1
A smaller share
Small cell (SCLC)
  • High-grade neuroendocrine tumor
  • Almost always in smokers
  • Fast-growing, with early spread and frequent brain metastases
  • Staged as limited vs extensive; treated with chemo ± RT, rarely surgery

The Three Histologies That Change Your Thinking

HistologyClassic pictureWhy it matters to you
AdenocarcinomaMost common NSCLC; often peripheral; the usual type in never-smokersMost often carries an actionable driver alteration, so molecular results can reshape systemic therapy at every stage.
Squamous cellStrong smoking association; often central; can cavitateCentral tumors bring the airway, esophagus, and mediastinum into the plan. Classically linked to PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.
Small cellHigh-grade neuroendocrine; rapid growth; early metastatic spreadTreatment is fundamentally different: systemic therapy is central even when the chest disease looks limited.

You'll also hear about large cell carcinoma (a poorly differentiated NSCLC, treated like other NSCLC) and carcinoid tumors (low-grade neuroendocrine tumors, usually managed surgically). Know they exist; they rarely drive the radiation oncology reasoning on a sub-I.

Squamous and small cell sit in the Center (both start with S). Adenocarcinoma lives at the edges.

Risk Factors

Smoking is the dominant risk factor, but it isn't the only one.

1
Tobacco

The dominant cause. Risk rises with pack-years and falls slowly after quitting, but never back to baseline. Secondhand smoke counts too.

2
Radon

The leading cause in never-smokers. A radioactive gas from soil that collects in basements.

3
Occupational

Asbestos (multiplies smoking risk rather than adding to it; also causes mesothelioma), silica, arsenic, chromium, nickel, diesel exhaust.

4
Personal History

Prior chest radiation (Hodgkin lymphoma, breast cancer), COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, HIV, family history, air pollution.

Clinical Pearl

A younger woman who never smoked with lung adenocarcinoma is the classic EGFR-mutant patient. Lung cancer in a never-smoker should make you think about a targetable driver before anything else in the systemic plan.

Driver Mutations and PD-L1: Why the Biopsy Goes Beyond Histology

Many NSCLCs, especially adenocarcinomas in never-smokers, are driven by a single alteration that a targeted drug can block. Testing (usually next-generation sequencing) plus PD-L1 staining is standard for nonsquamous NSCLC, and it now matters for early-stage and stage III disease, not only metastatic disease.

Driver-positive
Targeted therapy

An actionable alteration usually makes targeted therapy the main systemic strategy, sometimes before or after surgery or chemoradiation.

Driver-negative
Chemo and immunotherapy

Systemic therapy is guided by PD-L1, histology, stage, and the clinical context.

DriverWhy you should know it
EGFRTargetable, with major implications after surgery and after chemoradiation for stage III
ALKTargetable; the other classic never-smoker driver
KRAS G12CTargetable in advanced disease; more common in smokers
ROS1, RET, MET, BRAF, NTRK, HER2Other actionable alterations, each with a targeted option
When an actionable driver is present, targeted therapy often becomes the dominant systemic strategy; immunotherapy decisions depend on the specific alteration and the treatment setting.

From Biopsy to Radiation Plan

The pieces above fit together in one chain. Each step narrows the next:

1
Biopsy
→
2
Histology (NSCLC vs SCLC)
→
3
Stage
→
4
Molecular testing and PD-L1
→
5
Systemic therapy
→
6
Radiation strategy

For example, an EGFR-mutant stage III adenocarcinoma still gets chemoradiation, but the drug that follows it is different; small cell histology changes almost everything, from the radiation schedule to brain management.

Screening: Why You See So Many Small Peripheral Tumors

Because most lung cancers are silent until late, high-risk people are screened with low-dose CT (LDCT). Large trials (NLST in the US, NELSON in Europe) showed that screening lowers lung cancer deaths.

1
LDCT screening
→
2
Earlier-stage, often peripheral tumors
→
3
More patients eligible for cure with surgery or SBRT
  • USPSTF (2021): annual LDCT for ages 50-80 with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years.
  • Findings are reported with Lung-RADS, which sorts nodules into routine follow-up, short-interval CT, or PET/biopsy.
  • Many screen-detected patients have COPD or other comorbidities, which is why so many become SBRT patients.
Self-check: a 66-year-old quit 10 years ago after 30 pack-years. Does she qualify for screening? What if she quit 20 years ago?▾

Yes at 10 years (age 50-80, ≥20 pack-years, quit within 15 years). At 20 years she no longer meets USPSTF criteria, although some groups (e.g., the American Cancer Society, 2023) dropped the years-since-quitting limit.

How Lung Cancer Presents

More cancers are now found incidentally or on screening CT. When symptoms happen, they point to where the tumor is:

SymptomWhat it tells you
Cough, hemoptysis, post-obstructive pneumoniaCentral tumor in an airway
HoarsenessLeft recurrent laryngeal nerve in the AP window (T4)
Elevated hemidiaphragmPhrenic nerve invasion (T3)
Shoulder/arm pain, hand weakness, Horner syndromePancoast (superior sulcus) tumor
Face and arm swelling, dilated neck veinsSVC syndrome (often small cell or bulky right-sided nodes)
Dyspnea with an effusionPossible malignant effusion (M1a)
Headache, seizure, focal deficit; bone painBrain or bone metastases

Paraneoplastic Syndromes: Match the Syndrome to the Histology

Squamous cell
Hypercalcemia

Tumor secretes PTH-related peptide (PTHrP).

Small cell
Neuroendocrine

SIADH (hyponatremia), ectopic ACTH (Cushing), Lambert-Eaton (weakness that improves with use), cerebellar degeneration.

Adenocarcinoma
Clubbing & clots

Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing, painful joints) and hypercoagulability (Trousseau).

High-Yield Summary
  • Lung cancer is divided into non-small cell (mainly adenocarcinoma and squamous) and small cell, a high-grade neuroendocrine cancer that spreads early and is treated very differently.
  • Adenocarcinoma is often peripheral and is the usual type in never-smokers, while squamous and small cell cancers are often central and strongly tied to smoking.
  • Smoking is the main risk factor, and radon is the leading cause in never-smokers.
  • Nonsquamous NSCLC is tested for driver mutations and PD-L1, because an actionable driver often makes targeted therapy the main systemic strategy, and PD-L1 helps guide immunotherapy when there is none.
  • Low-dose CT screening finds earlier, often peripheral tumors, so more patients can be cured with surgery or SBRT.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Thoracic Anatomy & Lymph Node Stations
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
The next questions are where is it, and where can it spread? Thoracic anatomy answers both. Where the tumor sits (peripheral, central, apical, lower lobe) tells you what it can invade, which sets the T stage, and which organs the radiation plan will have to protect. Which lymph node stations are involved sets the N stage, which is often what decides between local therapy alone and multimodality treatment. This page has interactive modules for the lung and the lymph nodes; the mediastinal cross-sections are in the Imaging section, on real CT slices.

The Lung: Main Regions

Lobes, Fissures, and Segments

Right lung
3 lobes, 2 fissures
  • Upper, middle, lower lobes
  • Horizontal (minor) fissure: RUL vs RML
  • Oblique (major) fissure: RLL vs the rest
Left lung
2 lobes, 1 fissure
  • Upper (including the lingula) and lower lobes
  • Oblique fissure only
  • Smaller, to make room for the heart
  • Upper lobes get the most cancers. Lower lobes move the most with breathing, which matters for 4D-CT planning.
  • Surgeons think in lobes and segments: lobectomy is standard; segmentectomy is an option for small peripheral tumors.

Tumor Location Predicts Both Stage and Planning Risk

Once you know where the tumor is, you can predict what it might invade and what will limit the radiation plan:

LocationWhat it can invadeWhat the plan must protect
PeripheralVisceral pleuraSurrounding lung; the chest wall and ribs if it's close
Chest wallParietal pleura, ribs, intercostal musclesChest wall and ribs (pain, fracture)
CentralMain bronchus, mediastinum, great vessels, pericardiumProximal bronchial tree, esophagus, great vessels, heart
Apical (superior sulcus)First rib, brachial plexus, subclavian vessels, vertebral bodyBrachial plexus, spinal cord, vertebral body, subclavian vessels
Lower lobeDiaphragm (rarely)The main issue is respiratory motion, which has to be measured and controlled

Central vs Peripheral: A Spectrum, Not a Single Line

The proximal bronchial tree (PBT) is the trachea, carina, both main bronchi, and the lobar bronchi. Central tumors are generally defined by their proximity to the PBT and/or other critical mediastinal structures; the classic definition is within about 2 cm of the PBT, or touching the mediastinal or pericardial pleura. Ultracentral tumors directly abut or overlap critical structures such as the trachea, main bronchi, or esophagus. Definitions vary by protocol and institution, so learn the idea rather than a single cutoff.

The closer the tumor is to critical structures, the more fractionation and organ-at-risk limits shape the plan.

The Hilum and the Apex

  • Hilum (RALS): the pulmonary artery is Right Anterior, Left Superior relative to the main bronchus. Hilar nodes are station 10.
  • Apex / superior sulcus: the lung apex sits against the first rib, subclavian vessels, lower brachial plexus (C8-T1), and stellate ganglion. A tumor here is a Pancoast tumor: arm pain, hand weakness, and Horner syndrome. MRI shows what it invades.

The Thoracic Lymph Nodes

This is the most important map in thoracic oncology: the IASLC lymph node map. Nodal involvement, more than tumor size, often decides whether a patient is cured with local therapy alone.

What You Actually Need

You should be able to recognize the major stations on CT and understand how station involvement changes the N stage. You do not need to memorize every millimeter-level boundary; the table below is a reference for when you're looking at a scan or a nodal map.

The Numbering Rule

1
Station 1

Low cervical / supraclavicular. Always N3.

2-9
Single digits

Mediastinal. Ipsilateral = N2. Contralateral = N3.

10-14
Double digits

Hilar and intrapulmonary. Ipsilateral = N1. Contralateral = N3.

N1 = hilum (double digits) · N2 = same-side mediastinum (single digits) · N3 = across, or above the clavicle

Every Station at a Glance

StationNameRoughly whereN stage
1R / 1LLow cervical, supraclavicularAbove the clavicles and sternal notchN3 (either side)
2R / 2LUpper paratrachealBeside the upper tracheaN2 / N3
3a / 3pPrevascular / retrotrachealIn front of the great vessels / behind the tracheaN2 / N3
4R / 4LLower paratrachealBeside the lower trachea, down to the azygos (R) or left PA (L)N2 / N3
5Subaortic (AP window)Under the aortic archN2 if left tumor, N3 if right
6Para-aorticBeside the ascending aorta and archN2 if left tumor, N3 if right
7SubcarinalBelow the carinaN2 always
8ParaesophagealBeside the esophagus below the carinaN2 / N3
9Pulmonary ligamentAlong the inferior pulmonary ligamentN2 / N3
10HilarMain bronchus and hilar vesselsN1 / N3
11InterlobarBetween the lobar bronchiN1 / N3
12-14Lobar, segmental, subsegmentalInside the lungN1

The Staging Traps

Stations 5 and 6 are left-sided

A right-sided tumor with a station 5 or 6 node is N3.

Station 7 is always N2

It drains both lungs and is the most commonly involved mediastinal station.

The R/L line is off-center

The 2R/4R vs 2L/4L boundary is the left lateral wall of the trachea, not the midline.

Station 1 is N3, not M1

Supraclavicular nodes are N3 on either side. The patient can still be cured.

How Each Lobe Drains

  • Right upper lobe → 10R → 4R, 2R.
  • Left upper lobe → 5, 6 (AP window and para-aortic), then 4L.
  • Lower lobes (either side) → 7, 8, 9. Left lower lobe tumors can cross to the right paratracheal nodes.
  • Skip metastases (N2 without N1) are not rare, so an empty hilum doesn't clear the mediastinum.

Sampling the Nodes: EBUS vs Mediastinoscopy

CT and PET are imperfect: PET-positive nodes can be inflammatory, and a PET-negative mediastinum can still hide disease. If nodal status will change management, suspicious mediastinal disease generally needs pathologic confirmation.

ProcedureStations it reachesNotes
EBUS (endobronchial ultrasound)2R/2L, 4R/4L, 7, 10, 11Needle through the airway. Usually first; can reach hilar nodes.
EUS (through the esophagus)4L, 7, 8, 9Adds the lower stations.
Cervical mediastinoscopy2R/2L, 4R/4L, 7Surgical; used when EBUS is negative but suspicion remains.
Chamberlain / VATS5, 6Reaches the AP window and para-aortic nodes.
PET finds the nodes. EBUS proves them.
High-Yield Summary
  • Tumor location predicts both what the tumor can invade and which organs the radiation plan must protect.
  • Location sets the OARs: peripheral tumors bring the lung and chest wall, central tumors the airway, esophagus, heart, and great vessels, and apical tumors the brachial plexus and cord; lower lobe tumors move the most.
  • Central and ultracentral tumors are defined by how close they sit to the proximal bronchial tree and mediastinal structures, and exact definitions vary by protocol.
  • Hilar and intrapulmonary nodes (stations 10 to 14) are N1, ipsilateral mediastinal nodes (stations 2 to 9, including subcarinal station 7) are N2, and contralateral or supraclavicular nodes are N3.
  • If nodal status would change management, a suspicious mediastinal node needs tissue, usually by EBUS.

Imaging.title: Thoracic Imaging
Imaging.html:
The question for this page is what does each scan tell me? Imaging drives almost every thoracic decision: whether a nodule is cancer, how far it has spread, and exactly where the beam goes. Rather than learning pulmonary radiology, organize what you see around five questions, each answered by a different scan. This section comes before Workup & Staging because staging a lung cancer is mostly reading these scans.

QuestionMain scanWhen you'll see it
1. Is this lesion cancer?CT (low-dose CT for screening)Screening and incidental nodules
2. Where exactly is the primary?CT chest with contrast; MRI for apical tumorsEvery patient (include the upper abdomen for liver and adrenals)
3. Are the nodes involved?FDG PET/CT, then tissueEvery patient treated with curative intent
4. Is there distant disease?PET/CT plus brain MRIBrain MRI for stage II and above (consider for IB) and all SCLC
5. How does the tumor move?4D-CT simulationEvery lung radiation plan

Question 1: Is This Lesion Cancer?

The lung window (wide window, dark background) shows a nodule's margins, texture, and relationship to the airways and fissures.

Suspicious
Favors cancer
  • Growth over time
  • Spiculated or irregular margin
  • Larger size (over 3 cm is called a mass)
  • Upper lobe location
  • Part-solid texture
  • Smoking history
Reassuring
Favors benign
  • Smooth, well-defined margin
  • Benign calcification or fat inside
  • Stable for 2 years (solid nodule)
  • Small size in a low-risk person
  • Ground glass → part-solid → solid. The ground-glass part is usually non-invasive growth; the solid part is the invasive tumor, so the solid part sets the T stage.
  • Screening nodules are triaged with Lung-RADS: low risk goes back to annual CT, intermediate gets a short-interval CT, and suspicious goes to PET/CT or biopsy.

Question 2: Where Exactly Is the Primary?

On the contrast CT, describe the tumor the way the team will need it for staging and planning:

1
Which lobe?

Predicts the nodal drainage and how much the tumor will move.

2
Central or peripheral?

How close is it to the proximal bronchial tree, esophagus, and great vessels?

3
What does it touch?

Chest wall, mediastinum, airway, or the apex (plexus, vessels, vertebra).

Finding Your Level in the Mediastinum

You don't need to read the mediastinum like a radiologist, but you should recognize these four slices and the stations at each:

LevelHow you know you're thereNodal stations
1. Great vesselsSeveral round vessels in front of the trachea2R, 2L, 3a, 3p
2. Aortic archOne long vessel curving beside the trachea4R, 3a, 3p, 6
3. Pulmonary arteriesThe main pulmonary artery splitting; two separate main bronchi5, 7, 10R, 10L
4. HeartHeart chambers; the esophagus right behind the left atrium8, 9
Self-check: a left upper lobe patient is newly hoarse. Where is the problem, and what does it do to the T stage?▾

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch through the AP window, where tumor or station 5 nodes can trap it. Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement is T4.

The mediastinum is also split into prevascular, visceral, and paravertebral compartments. Lung cancer nodes live mostly in the visceral (middle) compartment; an anterior mass usually means something else (thymoma, lymphoma, germ cell tumor).

Question 3: Are the Nodes Involved?

  • On CT, a mediastinal node with a short axis over 1 cm is called enlarged, and a necrotic center strongly suggests tumor. But size alone is only moderately accurate: small nodes can hold cancer and big nodes can be reactive.
  • Always name the station (e.g., "enlarged 4R and 7"), not just "mediastinal adenopathy." The station and side decide N1 vs N2 vs N3.
  • PET/CT is the standard for nodal and distant staging and often upstages patients compared with CT alone.
  • Hot doesn't always mean cancer. Infection, TB, fungal disease, sarcoidosis, and recent surgery or RT all light up.
  • Cold doesn't always mean benign. Ground-glass adenocarcinoma, carcinoid, and very small nodes can be PET-negative.
  • For radiation, PET helps draw the GTV: it separates hot tumor from cooler atelectasis and shows which nodes belong in the target.
1
Enlarged or PET-avid node
→
2
Would it change treatment?
→
3
Tissue: EBUS or mediastinoscopy
→
4
N stage and treatment plan
PET finds the nodes. EBUS proves them. A PET-positive node gets tissue if it would change treatment.

Question 4: Is There Distant Disease?

PET/CT covers the body, but normal brain is always FDG-avid, so PET cannot screen the brain. That's what the contrast brain MRI is for.

MRI brain
Hunting metastases
  • For stage II-IV NSCLC (consider for IB) and every SCLC.
  • Metastases enhance, sit at the gray-white junction, and bring vasogenic edema.
  • One brain met makes it stage IV; a few small mets are usually treated with SRS.
MRI chest (back to Question 2)
Pancoast tumors
  • Shows the brachial plexus, subclavian vessels, neural foramina, and vertebral body better than CT.
  • Decides resectability and what the RT volume must include and avoid.
Clinical Pearl

An apical opacity called "pleural thickening" in a smoker with shoulder or inner-arm pain, hand weakness, or Horner syndrome is a Pancoast tumor until proven otherwise. Get a CT and an MRI.

Question 5: How Does the Tumor Move? 4D-CT and the Target

This is the radiation oncologist's scan, and the signature idea of thoracic planning: thoracic RT has to cover where the tumor will be throughout the breathing cycle, not just where it sits on one scan. A 4D-CT scans the patient in the treatment position (arms up) through the whole breathing cycle, so the team can see the tumor at full inhale, full exhale, and everything in between.

1
Tumor on inhale ↔ tumor on exhale
→
2
GTV in each phase
→
3
ITV: every position combined
→
4
PTV: ITV + setup margin
PTVThe ITV plus a small margin for daily setup uncertainty
ITVWhere the tumor moves during breathing: the GTV from every phase of the 4D-CT combined
GTVWhat we can see: the tumor on CT (lung window) and PET
When motion is large
  • Abdominal compression
  • Respiratory gating
  • Breath hold
  • Daily cone-beam CT
  • Lower lobe tumors move the most, because they sit on the diaphragm. When motion is large, the team uses abdominal compression, gating, or breath hold rather than simply making the target bigger.
  • Daily cone-beam CT lines up the tumor before each SBRT fraction.
  • For stage III chemoradiation, a CTV margin for microscopic spread is added before the PTV (see Treatment Paradigms).
Tumor motion is part of the target.

After SBRT: Fibrosis or Recurrence?

Nearly every SBRT patient develops radiation changes at the treated site: consolidation in the first months, then fibrosis that can look like a mass. Radiation fibrosis can look like recurrent tumor, so don't call recurrence too early.

Expected
Radiation fibrosis
  • Conforms to the high-dose region
  • Keeps air bronchograms
  • Most change early, then stabilizes or contracts
  • Linear or straight edges
Worrisome
Possible recurrence
  • New or progressively enlarging mass-like opacity, especially after the early post-treatment period
  • Bulging margin
  • Loss of air bronchograms
  • Craniocaudal growth

High-risk features like these should raise concern for recurrence and may prompt PET/CT and/or biopsy.

High-Yield Summary
  • Each scan answers one question: CT asks whether a lesion is cancer and where it is, PET/CT asks about nodes and distant disease, brain MRI looks for brain metastases, and 4D-CT shows how the tumor moves.
  • A suspicious nodule is growing, spiculated, larger, part-solid, or in an upper lobe, and in a part-solid nodule the solid part sets the T stage.
  • PET finds suspicious nodes, but a PET-positive node that would change treatment needs tissue, because infection and sarcoid can light up too.
  • Thoracic radiation has to cover where the tumor will be throughout the breathing cycle, so the GTV from each phase of the 4D-CT is combined into an ITV, and a setup margin makes the PTV.
  • Fibrosis after SBRT is expected, while a new or growing mass-like opacity, a bulging margin, or lost air bronchograms raise concern for recurrence and may prompt PET/CT or biopsy.

Workup & Staging.title: Lung Cancer Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
This page answers how do I turn this into a treatment-ready diagnosis? You don't need the whole AJCC manual. You need the workup that gets a patient to a stage, the shape of T, N, and M, and, most of all, which staging features change management. For every patient, answer four questions: How big is the primary? What does it invade? Where are the nodes? Has it spread? Then ask a fifth that the stage alone can't answer: can it be resected, and can this patient tolerate it?

Staging and Guideline Version

Staging uses the AJCC 9th edition (2024). Workup and treatment pathways are simplified summaries of the NCCN Non-Small Cell and Small Cell Lung Cancer Guidelines; this content was last revised in October 2026. Lung cancer pathways change quickly, so check the current guideline version for real patients. The NCCN workup and full staging tables are at the bottom of the page.

The Core Workup: What Every Patient Gets

  1. History and physical. Smoking history, weight loss, performance status, and symptoms that suggest invasion (hoarseness, arm pain, Horner) or metastases (headache, bone pain).
  2. Tissue diagnosis, choosing the biopsy that also gives the highest stage in one step.
  3. Biomarkers: molecular testing and PD-L1, which now matter for resectable and stage III disease, not just stage IV.
  4. CT chest with contrast, including the upper abdomen (liver and adrenals).
  5. FDG PET/CT for nodal and distant staging.
  6. MRI brain with contrast for stage II and higher (consider for IB) and for all small cell.
  7. Invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS ± mediastinoscopy) when nodal status would change management.
  8. Pulmonary function tests (FEV1 and DLCO) to decide who can tolerate surgery, and to plan radiation safely.
  9. Smoking cessation. Smoking during treatment worsens outcomes and toxicity.

Which Biopsy?

SituationBest first test
Peripheral nodule, no suspicious nodesCT-guided needle biopsy (or navigational bronchoscopy), or straight to surgery if suspicion is high and the patient is operable
Central tumorBronchoscopy with biopsy
Suspicious mediastinal or hilar nodesEBUS-guided needle aspiration: diagnoses and stages at once
Pleural effusionThoracentesis (positive = M1a)
Suspected single metastasisBiopsy the metastasis if it's easy to reach: it proves stage IV
Biopsy the site that gives the highest stage. One needle can diagnose and stage at the same time.

Who Needs Invasive Mediastinal Staging?

The principle: if nodal status will change management, suspicious mediastinal disease generally needs pathologic confirmation.

  • Usually yes: enlarged or PET-positive mediastinal nodes, PET-positive hilar nodes, central tumors, and larger tumors.
  • Often skipped: a small peripheral tumor with a clean PET/CT mediastinum.
  • Before SBRT, this matters just as much: SBRT treats the primary alone, so it only makes sense if the nodes are truly negative.

Can the Patient Tolerate Surgery?

FEV1 and DLCO help determine whether a patient can tolerate lung resection. Predicted postoperative values (what's left after removing the lobe) and exercise testing refine the assessment in borderline cases. Very poor lung function steers a node-negative patient toward SBRT.

Planning details: the usual PFT thresholds▾
  • Predicted postoperative (ppo) FEV1 and DLCO both over 60%: low risk, proceed to surgery.
  • Between about 30% and 60%: exercise testing (stair climb, VO2 max).
  • Under about 30%, or a very low VO2 max: high surgical risk, which favors SBRT.

What Each Part of the Stage Changes

T
Size matters, but invasion can upstage

Decides the extent of surgery, whether SBRT is feasible, and which organs sit next to the target.

N
The biggest treatment switch

N0 → local therapy (surgery or SBRT). N1 → multimodality therapy. N2/N3 → a major change in both the local and the systemic strategy.

M
Systemic therapy becomes central

M1 → systemic therapy leads, with selected patients still getting aggressive local therapy.

T: Size First, Then Invasion

TSize...or any of these features
T1≤3 cmSurrounded by lung or visceral pleura, not in the main bronchus
T2>3-5 cmVisceral pleura; main bronchus (not the carina); atelectasis/obstructive pneumonitis reaching the hilum
T3>5-7 cmChest wall (incl. parietal pleura, superior sulcus), phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium; separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cmMediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, vertebral body, diaphragm; separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe
Know the big cutoffs (3, 5, and 7 cm), then remember that invasion beats size.

In part-solid tumors, measure only the solid (invasive) part. The exact subcategories (T1a-c, T2a-b) are in the AJCC tables at the bottom.

The Nodule Rule

Separate tumor nodule in the same lobe → T3. Different lobe, same lung → T4. Other lung → M1a.

Quick check: a 2.5 cm right lower lobe tumor invades the visceral pleura. What's the T stage?▾

T2. Size alone would say T1, but visceral pleural invasion makes it T2. Always check for invasion before locking in T from size.

Quick check: a 3.5 cm tumor has invaded the phrenic nerve. T3 or T4?▾

T3. Phrenic nerve, chest wall, and parietal pericardium are T3. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is T4. (Phrenic = paralyzed diaphragm; recurrent laryngeal = hoarseness.)

N: Where Are the Nodes?

The Anatomy section has the full station map. Here's the staging version:

NDefinitionThink
N0No regional nodes
N1Ipsilateral hilar, peribronchial, intrapulmonary (stations 10-14)Same side, double digits
N2aSingle ipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal stationSame side, one single-digit station
N2bMultiple ipsilateral mediastinal stationsSame side, two or more single-digit stations
N3Contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene/supraclavicularAcross, or above the clavicle

"N2" vs N2a and N2b: clinically, you will often hear "N2" used broadly. The AJCC 9th edition subdivides N2 into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations) because the distinction carries prognostic weight and comes up in resectability discussions.

Why the nodes matter so much: a T1N0 and a T1N2 tumor can be the same size, but the nodes move the patient from "surgery or SBRT" to "multimodality therapy." N2 pattern influences resectability, but it doesn't decide it alone (see below).

Quick check: right upper lobe tumor with PET-positive, EBUS-proven 4R and 7 nodes. What N?▾

N2b. Both are ipsilateral mediastinal stations (7 always counts as ipsilateral), and there are two stations, so it's N2b rather than N2a.

M: The Part That Changes Everything

MMeaningExamples
M1aSpread within the chestContralateral lung nodule, pleural or pericardial nodules, malignant pleural/pericardial effusion
M1bSingle extrathoracic metastasisOne brain met, one adrenal met
M1cMultiple extrathoracic metastases (M1c1 in one organ system, M1c2 in several)Several bone mets; liver and bone mets

Once a patient is M1, systemic therapy becomes central. But a patient with one or a few metastases (oligometastatic) may still get aggressive local therapy, such as SBRT to every site, alongside systemic therapy.

Stage ≠ Resectability ≠ Operability

This is the distinction that most often trips up students. Three different questions, answered by different people:

1
Stage

How far has the disease spread? Comes from imaging and pathology.

2
Resectability

Can surgery achieve an appropriate oncologic (complete) resection with acceptable morbidity? A question about the tumor's anatomy and nodal burden.

3
Operability

Can this patient tolerate the operation? Lung function, heart disease, frailty, and performance status.

Stage tells you the extent of disease. Resectability asks whether surgery can remove it appropriately. Operability asks whether the patient can survive the operation.
  • A stage IIIA T3N1 tumor may be fully resectable in a fit patient: surgery-based treatment.
  • Another stage IIIA patient with bulky, multi-station mediastinal nodes may be unresectable: definitive chemoradiation.
  • A stage IA tumor is easily resectable, but in a patient with severe COPD it is inoperable: SBRT.
1
Full staging
→
2

→
3
Surgery-based treatment or definitive chemoradiation

Worked Example

Worked Example
Patient

CT: 2.8 cm right upper lobe mass. PET: right hilar (10R) node, no mediastinal nodes, no distant disease. Brain MRI negative.

Your thought process

Tumor 2.8 cm, no invasion → T1c. Ipsilateral hilar node → N1. No metastases → M0. T1c N1 M0 = Stage IIA.

Now change one thing

The PET shows a single 4R node instead of the hilar node. T1c N2a M0 = Stage IIB. Add a subcarinal node too: T1c N2b M0 = Stage IIIA. Same primary, three different stages, three different conversations. That's why the nodes matter.

Try It: Stage These Patients

Work out the T, N, M, and stage group before checking. They get harder.

CT: 2.1 cm peripheral left upper lobe nodule. PET: no nodal or distant uptake.

Answer: T1c N0 M0, Stage IA3. Small, peripheral, N0: the textbook surgery or SBRT patient.

CT: 2.4 cm right lower lobe tumor with a separate small nodule in the same lobe. PET: no nodal or distant uptake.

Answer: T3 N0 M0, Stage IIB. A separate nodule in the same lobe is T3 by definition. Size alone would have misled you.

CT: 4.5 cm right upper lobe mass. PET/EBUS: positive subcarinal (7) node only.

Answer: T2b N2a M0, Stage IIIA. Station 7 is single-digit (mediastinal) and always counts as ipsilateral: N2, and only one station, so N2a. This one station moves the patient from a surgery/SBRT discussion into a multimodality one.

CT: 3.2 cm right upper lobe tumor. PET/EBUS: positive 4R and an FDG-avid station 5 node, confirmed by VATS biopsy.

Answer: T2a N3 M0, Stage IIIB. Station 5 is a left-sided station, so for a right tumor it's contralateral: N3.

CT: 5.5 cm left hilar mass. PET: ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal nodes. MRI brain: one cerebellar metastasis.

Answer: T3 N2 M1b, Stage IVA. A single extrathoracic metastasis is M1b and makes it stage IV no matter the T and N. This patient might still get SRS to the brain met and aggressive treatment of the chest (oligometastatic approach).

Small Cell Lung Cancer: Limited vs Extensive

SCLC is formally staged with the same TNM system, but treatment follows the older two-stage system:

Curative intent
Limited stage (LS)

Confined to one hemithorax and its regional nodes, and can be covered by one tolerable radiation field. Roughly TNM stage I-III.

Goal: cure with concurrent chemoradiation.

Most patients
Extensive stage (ES)

Anything beyond that: distant metastases, a malignant effusion, or disease too large for one field.

Goal: control with chemo-immunotherapy, with RT for select responders and symptoms.

SCLC workup adds a brain MRI for everyone (brain metastases are common) and, for the rare T1-2 N0 patient being considered for surgery, invasive mediastinal staging first.

High-Yield Summary
  • Workup is a tissue diagnosis with molecular testing, CT chest and upper abdomen, PET/CT, brain MRI for stage II and above, mediastinal staging when it would change management, and PFTs.
  • In T staging, size matters, but invasion of the chest wall, mediastinum, or other structures can upstage a small tumor.
  • The N stage most often changes treatment: N0 disease gets local therapy, N1 disease gets multimodality therapy, and N2 or N3 disease changes both the local and systemic strategy.
  • Stage, resectability, and operability are different questions, and a multidisciplinary tumor board decides between surgery-based treatment and definitive chemoradiation.
  • Small cell lung cancer is staged as limited (fits in one tolerable radiation field) or extensive.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Lung Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
This page answers the real sub-I question: I have a lung cancer patient in front of me. Do they need surgery, SBRT, chemoradiation, systemic therapy, or a combination? And if we're using radiation, what exactly goes in the field, and what are we trying to protect? Almost every decision comes from three questions, asked in this order:

1
What is the stage?

Above all, the nodes. N0 → treat the primary. N1-N3 → multimodality therapy. M1 → systemic therapy leads. Small cell follows its own path.

2
Is the disease resectable, and is the patient operable?

Two separate questions. Resectable and operable → surgery-based treatment. Either answer is no → SBRT (N0) or chemoradiation (node-positive).

3
If we use RT, what does the location require us to protect?

Peripheral, chest wall, apical, central, or ultracentral. Location sets the fractionation and the toxicity you're guarding against.

Guideline Version

Pathways here are simplified summaries of the NCCN Non-Small Cell and Small Cell Lung Cancer Guidelines with AJCC 9th edition staging, last revised in October 2026. Thoracic oncology is changing quickly, especially systemic therapy, so check the current guideline version for real patients.

The page follows the patient: the framework, the roles of surgery and systemic therapy, then each paradigm from early N0 disease to stage III, metastatic disease, and small cell. Then what the radiation plan actually treats, the toxicities it is built to avoid, and the NCCN tables.

The Framework: Who Gets What

The NSCLC treatment framework

Find the first step that fits your patient.

1
If the tumor is…
N0 (stage I-II), resectable, and the patient is operable
Lobectomy (or segmentectomy for small peripheral tumors) with lymph node sampling. Systemic therapy for larger tumors or if nodes turn up positive.
Surgery is the standard for fit patients. No routine radiation after a complete resection.
2
If the tumor is…
N0 and the patient is medically inoperable (or declines surgery)
SBRT, with fractionation adapted to location: peripheral, chest wall, central, or ultracentral.
High local control. No chemotherapy.
3
If the nodes are…
N1, or N2 that tumor board judges resectable
Neoadjuvant/perioperative systemic therapy → surgery (targeted therapy if EGFR/ALK). Inoperable → concurrent chemoRT.
SBRT treats the primary only, so it is not used for node-positive disease.
4
If the disease is…
Unresectable stage III (often bulky or multi-station N2, N3, or T4 invading the mediastinum)
Concurrent chemoRT, 60 Gy in 30 fractions → consolidation systemic therapy (durvalumab, or osimertinib if EGFR-mutant).
PACIFIC and LAURA. Don't escalate past 60 Gy (RTOG 0617).
5
If the patient has…
Metastatic disease (M1)
Systemic therapy (targeted or chemo-immunotherapy) + SBRT for selected oligometastatic sites or palliative RT for symptoms.
Try it: T1c N0, peripheral, FEV1 35%. Which step?▾

Step 2: SBRT. The tumor is resectable, but the patient is not operable. Peripheral, so a short, highly ablative course works.

Try it: same tumor, but EBUS shows a positive 4R node and the patient is still inoperable. What changes?▾

Concurrent chemoradiation (T1c N2a, stage IIB, but node-positive and inoperable). SBRT is off the table once nodes are positive; the involved nodes need to be in the field.

The Role of Surgery

  • Lobectomy with a lymph node dissection or systematic sampling is the standard operation.
  • Segmentectomy is now an accepted standard for small (≤2 cm) peripheral, N0 tumors: CALGB 140503 showed it was noninferior to lobectomy, and JCOG0802 showed better overall survival with segmentectomy.
  • Pneumonectomy is avoided when possible, especially after chemoradiation.
  • Positive margin (R1/R2) → re-resection if possible, otherwise postoperative RT (± chemo).
  • Surgery vs SBRT for early stage has never been settled by a completed large randomized trial. Surgery stays standard for fit patients; for medically inoperable patients or selected patients who decline surgery, definitive SBRT is a standard curative option.

The Role of Systemic Therapy

SettingWhat's givenKey trial
With definitive RT (stage III)Concurrent platinum doublet: a radiosensitizer and systemic therapyConcurrent beats sequential
After chemoRTDurvalumab × 12 months; osimertinib if EGFR-mutantPACIFIC, LAURA
Before surgeryChemo + immunotherapy ± continued after surgeryCheckMate 816, KEYNOTE-671
After surgeryChemo for higher-risk disease; targeted therapy (EGFR, ALK) or immunotherapy by biomarkerADAURA, ALINA, IMpower010
With SBRT (stage I)None routinely
MetastaticTargeted therapy if an actionable driver; otherwise chemo-immunotherapy or immunotherapy guided by PD-L1
Chemo is given WITH radiation in stage III (concurrent), and BEFORE or AFTER surgery. It is not added to SBRT for early-stage disease.

Paradigm 1: Early-Stage N0, Peripheral

The most common patient you'll see: a small, peripheral, node-negative tumor, often found on screening, in a patient with bad COPD.

  1. Confirm it's really N0: PET/CT, plus EBUS if the tumor is central, larger, or PET shows any suspicious nodes.
  2. Resectable and operable: lobectomy or segmentectomy.
  3. Medically inoperable, or declines surgery: definitive SBRT, a highly ablative course in a few fractions (for example, 54 Gy in 3 fractions). A biopsy is preferred, but treatment without one can be reasonable when the nodule is growing, PET-avid, and too risky to biopsy.

SBRT uses a highly ablative biologic dose delivered in a small number of fractions, with the fractionation adjusted for how close the tumor is to critical structures. The main side effect is usually mild pneumonitis.

RTOG 0236

SBRT for inoperable peripheral stage I NSCLC controlled the primary tumor in nearly all patients at 3 years.

Paradigm 2: Chest Wall and Apex

Abutting the chest wall
SBRT is still standard
  • Risk: chest wall pain and rib fracture
  • More fractions may be used to reduce chest wall and rib toxicity
Invading the chest wall (T3)
En bloc resection
  • Operable: en bloc resection of the lung and chest wall
  • Inoperable: SBRT (if small, N0) or definitive chemoRT

Superior Sulcus (Pancoast) Tumors

1
MRI + full staging
→
2
Neoadjuvant chemoRT
→
3
Surgery
→
4
More systemic therapy

If the tumor is unresectable (extensive plexus or vertebral invasion), it gets definitive chemoradiation. Either way, the brachial plexus and spinal cord sit right next to the target and limit the plan.

SWOG 9416 / INT 0160

Induction chemoRT then surgery gave a complete (R0) resection in most Pancoast tumors, establishing the trimodality approach.

Paradigm 3: Central and Ultracentral

As the tumor gets closer to the airway, esophagus, and great vessels, those organs, not the tumor, start to set the plan.

Central
More fractions
  • Near the proximal bronchial tree or mediastinal structures
  • Three-fraction SBRT is generally avoided because of the risk of severe toxicity; safer regimens use more fractions (for example, 50 Gy in 5)
  • If the tumor invades the mediastinum (T4), it's not an SBRT case: resection after induction if operable, otherwise definitive chemoRT
Ultracentral
OAR limits dominate
  • Tumor or PTV directly abuts or overlaps the trachea, main bronchi, or esophagus
  • The optimal regimen is not universal; fractionation is individualized around airway, esophageal, and vascular limits, sometimes with conventional fractionation
  • The fear is fatal hemoptysis and fistula, so organ limits are respected even if part of the PTV is underdosed
Indiana phase II (Timmerman)

Central tumors treated in 3 fractions had a much higher risk of severe toxicity, which created the idea of a "no-fly zone" around the proximal bronchial tree.

RTOG 0813

Central tumors tolerated 5-fraction SBRT with high local control.

HILUS

SBRT to tumors next to the main bronchi and trachea caused a high rate of fatal toxicity, mostly bleeding.

LocationHow SBRT adaptsMain worry
PeripheralHighly ablative, short coursePneumonitis
Chest wallMore fractions may be usedRib fracture, chest wall pain
CentralMore fractions; airway and mediastinal limitsAirway, great vessels, esophagus
UltracentralEven more caution; OAR limits may dominateFatal hemoptysis, fistula
The closer to the middle of the chest, the more fractions, and the more the organs at risk drive the plan.

Paradigm 4: Node-Positive, Hilar (N1)

  • Resectable and operable: lobectomy + nodal dissection with systemic therapy before and/or after surgery (chemo-immunotherapy, or targeted therapy by biomarker).
  • Inoperable: concurrent chemoRT, as for stage III. SBRT alone does not treat the nodes.
  • N1 or N2 found unexpectedly at surgery: finish the resection, then adjuvant systemic therapy. No routine PORT with negative margins.

Paradigm 5: Mediastinal Nodes, Stage III (N2-N3)

The first question for every stage III patient: resectable or not? Tumor board decides before anything starts.

N2 pattern influences resectability, but resectability is a multidisciplinary judgment based on nodal burden, tumor anatomy, surgical expertise, response to systemic therapy, and expected morbidity, not N stage alone.
Resectable
Surgery-based
  • Selected patients, often with limited, non-bulky N2, or T3-4 N0-1
  • Neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, then surgery ± adjuvant therapy
  • Radiation mainly for a positive margin
Unresectable
Definitive chemoradiation
  • Often bulky or multi-station N2, N3, or T4 invading the mediastinum
  • 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent platinum chemo
  • Then consolidation: durvalumab, or osimertinib if EGFR-mutant
  • Too frail for concurrent chemo: sequential chemo then RT, or RT alone.
  • PORT is for a positive margin, not routinely for resected N2 with clear margins.
RTOG 0617

74 Gy was worse than 60 Gy for survival, and heart dose predicted death. 60 Gy is the standard.

PACIFIC / LAURA

Durvalumab after chemoRT improved survival; osimertinib replaces it for EGFR-mutant tumors.

CheckMate 816

Adding nivolumab to chemo before surgery greatly increased the rate of complete pathologic response.

LungART

PORT after complete resection of N2 disease did not improve disease-free survival and added heart and lung toxicity.

Try it: T2a N2b (4R + 7), bulky nodes judged unresectable, EGFR wild-type, PD-L1 60%. Plan?▾

Concurrent chemoRT to 60 Gy/30 covering the primary and the involved 4R and 7 nodes, then durvalumab for 12 months.

Paradigm 6: Metastatic Disease

Systemic therapy leads. Radiation plays two roles:

Oligometastatic
Treat every site
  • A few metastases that are stable or responding on systemic therapy
  • SBRT to all sites (local consolidative therapy) + continue systemic therapy
  • Gomez (phase II) and SABR-COMET showed better survival with local therapy to every site in selected patients
  • Limited brain mets → SRS
Symptomatic
Palliative RT
  • Hemoptysis, airway obstruction, SVC syndrome, bone pain, cord compression, brain mets
  • Short courses, from a single fraction to about 2 weeks
  • Pick the course by prognosis and goals, not stage
The Key Reflex

"Metastatic lung cancer with worsening hemoptysis" does not mean 6 weeks of chemoradiation. First ask: what is the goal? Usually palliation, with a short course.

Paradigm 7: Small Cell Lung Cancer

Why Small Cell Is Treated Differently

SCLC is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive but tends to disseminate early. So systemic therapy is central even when the chest disease looks limited, radiation is added for local control, and the brain needs its own plan.

Limited stage
Curative intent
  • Platinum/etoposide + concurrent thoracic RT, started early
  • Then consolidation immunotherapy (durvalumab)
  • Brain management: PCI or MRI surveillance
  • Very early T1-2 N0 (rare): surgery + chemo
Extensive stage
Systemic therapy first
  • Platinum/etoposide + immunotherapy
  • Selected consolidative thoracic RT for good responders
  • Brain: MRI surveillance or PCI depending on context
  • Palliative RT as needed
Turrisi / CONVERT

Twice-daily thoracic RT (45 Gy in 30 fractions) beat once-daily RT to the same dose; CONVERT then found a higher once-daily dose about equal.

ADRIATIC

Durvalumab after chemoRT improved survival in limited-stage small cell.

What Are We Actually Treating?

You don't need to contour on a sub-I, but you should know what the team is drawing and why. The key difference between the two big thoracic plans is the nodes.

Early-Stage SBRT

PTVITV plus a small setup margin
ITVThe tumor's full range of breathing motion from the 4D-CT
GTVThe primary tumor only; no elective nodes

  • Esophagus

  • Heart
  • Spinal cord
  • Brachial plexus (apical)

Stage III Definitive Chemoradiation

No routine elective nodal irradiation in NSCLC: the field covers the primary and the involved nodes, which keeps lung, esophagus, and heart dose down.

Thoracic RT Toxicity: Know What You're Protecting

Every organ at risk in the plan maps to a side effect you'll counsel patients about. Knowing that link is what makes the plan make sense.

Acute (during and just after RT)
  • Esophagitis (painful swallowing), mainly with conventional chemoRT
  • Fatigue
  • Cough
  • Skin reaction, occasionally
  • Low blood counts, depending on the field and the chemo
Subacute and late (months to years)
  • Radiation pneumonitis (usually 1 to 6 months after RT)
  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • Esophageal stricture (rare)
  • Cardiac toxicity
  • Brachial plexopathy
  • Rib fracture and chest wall pain
  • Airway injury or bleeding after high-dose central or ultracentral treatment

Chest wall and ribsChest wall pain and rib fracture

High-Yield Summary
  • Early-stage, node-negative NSCLC gets surgery if it is resectable and the patient is operable, and SBRT is a standard curative option for medically inoperable patients or those who decline surgery.
  • SBRT fractionation is adjusted to location, with more fractions as the tumor gets closer to the chest wall, airway, esophagus, and great vessels.
  • Unresectable stage III NSCLC gets 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent chemo, followed by consolidation durvalumab, or osimertinib if EGFR-mutant.
  • NSCLC radiation treats the primary and involved nodes without routine elective nodal irradiation, while protecting the lungs, esophagus, heart, spinal cord, and brachial plexus.
  • Limited-stage small cell gets platinum and etoposide with early concurrent thoracic radiation, consolidation immunotherapy, and a brain plan, while extensive stage starts with chemo-immunotherapy.
